overview: IAG is a Spanish-incorporated, London/Madrid-listed holding company for a portfolio of flag-carrier and low-cost airlines: British Airways, Iberia, Vueling, Aer Lingus, LEVEL, plus IAG Cargo and the high-margin IAG Loyalty (Avios) business. The Group operates a hub-and-spoke network concentrated at London Heathrow and Madrid Barajas, connecting Europe to North America, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia, with secondary bases in Barcelona (Vueling) and Dublin (Aer Lingus). It is one of the largest airline groups in the world by revenue, and management targets sustainable 12-15% operating margins and 13-16% return on invested capital across the cycle.

business_model.summary: IAG earns the large majority of revenue from scheduled passenger flying (long-haul premium transatlantic/Latin America plus European short-haul), supplemented by cargo belly-hold capacity and a fast-growing, capital-light loyalty/co-brand business (IAG Loyalty, which runs the Avios points currency and British Airways Holidays). Passenger revenue is largely transactional (ticket-by-flight) rather than recurring, though corporate travel contracts and the loyalty ecosystem add some repeat-customer stickiness; deferred revenue from ticket sales and Avios points provides a float. Revenue is highly seasonal (H2/summer stronger) and cyclical with GDP/consumer and business travel spend.

revenue_streams.name: Other revenue (IAG Loyalty, Holidays, MRO, handling)

business_model.customer_type: B2C leisure and premium/business travelers across all airline brands, plus B2B corporate travel contracts and loyalty-program partners (banks, retailers) for Avios
business_model.geographic_mix: North Atlantic ~28-31% of capacity (ASKs), Latin America & Caribbean ~21-23%, Europe (incl. Domestic Spain/UK) ~31-33%, Africa/Middle East/South Asia ~11-13%, Asia Pacific ~5%. Revenue by airline brand roughly: British Airways largest (~55-60% of Group operating profit), Iberia strongly profitable second, Vueling and Aer Lingus smaller, LEVEL niche low-cost long-haul.

competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'Big Three' European network airline groups alongside Lufthansa Group and Air France-KLM; British Airways holds a dominant slot position at capacity-constrained London Heathrow and is the leading transatlantic carrier via its joint business with American Airlines; Iberia is a leading Europe-Latin America carrier from Madrid; Vueling and LEVEL compete in short-haul/low-cost long-haul niches; Aer Lingus is the leading Ireland-North Atlantic carrier but the Group's weakest-margin unit.

moat_factors.description: British Airways' entrenched slot portfolio at supply-constrained Heathrow (and Iberia at Madrid) is a durable structural barrier to new entrants and caps competitors' ability to contest IAG's core hubs
Joint venture with American Airlines and Finnair/Aer Lingus across the Atlantic allows revenue and cost coordination, supporting premium pricing on the most profitable long-haul corridor

Avios points currency with bank and retail partners creates switching costs for premium/frequent flyers and generates high-margin, capital-light, growing profit (>10%/year growth, targeting ~€1bn operating profit medium-term)
Multiple brands across premium long-haul, low-cost short-haul and regional markets reduce reliance on any single market or customer segment versus single-brand peers

Multi-year digital, commercial-systems and fleet-renewal transformation (BA.com rebuild, Iberia A321XLR growth, Vueling's Boeing fleet switch) is delivering unit-cost and revenue-management gains, though this is a self-improvement effort rather than a hard barrier to competitors

weaknesses: Aer Lingus materially underperforms Group margin targets, requiring restructuring (500 jobs cut, 6% capacity reduction, base closures)
Short-haul European markets are intensely competitive against lower-cost Ryanair/easyJet/Wizz Air, limiting fare/yield recovery when costs rise
Heavy fixed-cost base (aircraft, crew, fuel) means operating leverage cuts both ways; margins are sensitive to small revenue/cost swings
Heathrow capacity constraints and high airport charges limit British Airways' own growth even as the slot scarcity protects it from competitors
Reliance on partner airlines (e.g., Qatar Airways for Avios redemption inventory) outside IAG's direct control

growth_drivers: IAG Loyalty (Avios) targeted to reach ~£1 billion operating profit in the medium term, growing profit at >10%/year on a high-margin, capital-light basis

Iberia's 'Plan de Vuelo 2030' network growth via A321XLR long-haul narrowbody expansion (new Toronto, Newark, Recife, Fortaleza routes), targeting €1.4bn operating profit at the upper end of Group margin range
British Airways commercial/digital transformation (new booking platform, app, revenue management and payments systems) driving revenue and cost improvements
Premium short-haul strategy at Heathrow to improve short-haul yields rather than compete purely on price
Vueling's 'Project Rumbo' 10-year plan to reach 60 million passengers/year with a new Boeing 737 fleet replacing Airbus, improving unit costs
Fleet modernization (A321XLR, 787, 737 deliveries) improving fuel efficiency and unit costs across all airlines
Continued strong structural demand for international travel, particularly premium transatlantic and Latin American corridors
Disciplined capital allocation: ongoing share buybacks (€1.5bn excess-cash return programme announced Feb 2026) and growing dividend
Potential long-term benefit from Heathrow expansion (third runway, via either Heathrow's or the Arora 'Heathrow West' plan) if a workable charging model is agreed

business.description: Group's weakest-margin airline is undergoing a major restructuring (500 job cuts, 6% capacity reduction, base closures) to reach Group margin targets; execution risk remains
European low-cost carriers (Ryanair, easyJet, Wizz Air) are growing capacity aggressively in markets Vueling, Iberia and British Airways short-haul compete in, limiting pricing power
A large share of Group profit comes from premium transatlantic and Latin American long-haul; any slowdown in premium/corporate travel demand would disproportionately hit earnings

business.risk: Operational disruption (IT, air traffic control, strikes)
business.description: Legacy and new IT systems, European air traffic control strikes/congestion, and periodic labour disputes across multiple unionized workforces can cause costly cancellations

financial.description: Jet fuel is one of the largest cost lines; FY2026 fuel cost guided at roughly €8.3-8.6bn, up sharply versus prior guidance due to the Middle East conflict; Group recovers only ~60% of fuel cost increases through pricing/cost actions

Revenue and costs are generated in multiple currencies (EUR, GBP, USD and others); sterling/dollar/euro moves affect reported results and unit costs (FX contributed a modelled ~1pt benefit to FY2026 non-fuel unit costs)

financial.risk: High leverage/debt load from aircraft financing
financial.description: Borrowings of roughly €13.9bn as of mid-2026, though net leverage (0.6x EBITDA) and liquidity (~€11.9bn) are currently strong versus the <1.8x net leverage target
Material defined-benefit pension assets/obligations (particularly British Airways legacy schemes) create balance-sheet and funding volatility

regulatory.risk: Heathrow airport charges and expansion uncertainty
regulatory.description: IAG has said it will not back Heathrow's full third-runway expansion without an overhaul of the airport charging model; competing Arora 'Heathrow West' and Heathrow Ltd proposals create planning and cost uncertainty into the 2030s

EU Emissions Trading System extension proposals and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) mandates in the UK/EU raise compliance costs; IAG is lobbying for a globally consistent approach (CORSIA) and SAF supply/price support

regulatory.risk: Air passenger rights and compensation regimes (EC261/UK261)
regulatory.description: Disruption-related compensation obligations add cost volatility, particularly during the kind of geopolitical/airspace disruption seen in 2026
Any reform of historic slot allocation rules at Heathrow or other hubs could erode British Airways' and Iberia's structural advantage

macro.risk: Middle East conflict and airspace closures
macro.description: Conflict involving Iran/Gulf states/Israel has forced suspension of flights to the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Israel and Jordan (~3% of Group capacity) since Q1 2026, driving higher fuel prices, redeployed capacity and lower full-year profit versus original guidance; suspensions were extended through at least late October 2026
Passenger airlines are highly cyclical; a downturn in consumer discretionary and corporate travel spend would hit premium cabin and leisure demand
Aircraft financing and leasing costs are sensitive to interest rates, though net leverage is currently low and much of the fleet is unencumbered

macro.risk: Geopolitical disruption beyond the Middle East
macro.description: Precedent set by the current conflict shows the Group's broader exposure to airspace closures, sanctions, and route suspensions from future geopolitical shocks

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global air travel demand has remained structurally resilient through 2025-2026 despite geopolitical shocks, with premium/corporate travel and transatlantic/Latin American long-haul particularly strong; European short-haul capacity growth from low-cost carriers is outpacing demand in some markets, pressuring yields
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - airlines are classic cyclical, discretionary-spend businesses with high fixed costs and significant operating leverage; demand, especially premium and business travel, tracks GDP and corporate profit cycles closely
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - aircraft financing/leasing costs and discount rates on pension and lease liabilities are rate-sensitive, but IAG's net leverage (0.6x EBITDA) is currently low and liquidity strong
key_input_costs: Labour (pilots, cabin crew, ground staff - heavily unionized)
Airport and air traffic control charges (notably Heathrow)
Carbon/emissions allowances and Sustainable Aviation Fuel

recent_developments.event: Middle East route suspensions (Dubai, Doha, Tel Aviv, Bahrain, Amman, Riyadh) extended through at least late October 2026; British Airways permanently dropped Jeddah and redeployed capacity toward India, Africa and Asia

H1 2026 results: revenue up 1.0% to €16,064m, operating profit before exceptionals down 6.4% to €1,757m (margin 10.9% vs 11.8% H1 2025) as fuel cost increases outpaced pricing/cost mitigation; free cash flow strong at €2,905m; net leverage 0.6x
Aer Lingus announced major transformation/restructuring: ~6% flying-schedule reduction, voluntary departures, Manchester base closure, aimed at restoring Group-target margins within a few years
IAG Loyalty investor day (3 June 2026) showcased Avios/loyalty growth strategy, targeting ~€1bn operating profit in the medium term; H1 2026 Loyalty operating profit up 25% to £239m

IAG, Virgin Atlantic and IATA publicly backed Arora Group's revised 'Heathrow West' third-runway proposal as a credible alternative to Heathrow Ltd's £49bn plan, continuing to demand airport-charging model reform before supporting any expansion
Group executed a tender offer to repurchase its €825m 2028 convertible bond and issued €1,000m of new senior unsecured bonds (2031/2034 tranches), extending maturities and avoiding dilution

Q1 2026 results: revenue up 1.9% to €7,181m, operating profit up 77.3% to €351m (margin 4.9%); management flagged full-year profit would be lower than original guidance due to the Middle East conflict's fuel-price impact, while reaffirming the €1bn remaining excess-cash return programme

FY2025 results (record year): revenue up 3.5% to €33,213m, operating profit before exceptionals up 13.1% to €5,024m (margin 15.1%), adjusted EPS up 22.4% to 69.5€ cents, ROIC 18.5%; announced a further €1.5bn excess-cash return (starting with a €500m buyback) and raised the dividend 8.9%; shares fell ~5% on cautious Q2/Q3 2026 visibility commentary from the CFO
Vueling launched 'Project Rumbo,' a 10-year plan targeting 60 million passengers/year, with fleet transition from Airbus to Boeing 737 beginning late 2026

guidance.as_of: H1 2026 Results (August 2026) and Q1 2026 Trading Update (May 2026)

items.notes: Reaffirmed medium-term target range despite Middle East headwinds; H1 2026 delivered 10.9%
Cut from original ~3% growth guided at FY2025 results (Feb 2026), then further reduced through the year due to Middle East route suspensions and margin discipline

Sharply higher than original FY2025-results guidance of ~€7.0-7.4bn (62% hedged), driven by Middle East conflict; Group expects to recover ~60% of the fuel cost increase through revenue/cost actions, hedging policy unchanged
Reflects lower capacity growth than previously guided; delivered in line with guidance in H1
Down from ~€3.6bn guided in Feb 2026 and ~€3.5bn guided in May 2026; 16 aircraft now expected to be delivered in 2026 (one 787-10 slipped to 2027)

items.target: Significant, but below the >€3.0bn originally guided
items.notes: FY2025-results guidance was 'exceed €3.0bn'; Q1 2026 update said FY2026 FCF would be lower than that due to the Middle East conflict's profit impact, though still 'significant'
Actual net leverage was 0.6x at H1 2026, well within target
FY2025 actual RoIC was 18.5%, above the top of the target range

items.target: Complete remaining ~€1 billion of the €1.5 billion excess-cash return programme by end-February 2027 (c.€800m of the €1.5bn buyback completed by August 2026)
items.notes: Programme announced February 2026; management reaffirmed commitment despite lower FY2026 profit outlook

items.target: >10% per year, targeting ~€1 billion operating profit in the medium term
items.notes: H1 2026 reported profit grew 25% (partly timing benefits); underlying growth trajectory still >10%/year per management

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Luis Gallego has repeatedly stressed that IAG's diverse brand/market portfolio, structurally high margins, and strong balance sheet make it 'uniquely positioned' to absorb the Middle East conflict's fuel-cost shock without abandoning medium-term margin, RoIC and leverage targets or shareholder returns. CFO José Antonio Barrionuevo (and predecessor Nicholas Cadbury at the FY2025 results) flagged reduced visibility into Q2/Q3 2026 trading and guided that FY2026 profit and free cash flow would be lower than originally planned, while reiterating that around 60% of the higher fuel cost would be recovered through pricing and cost initiatives and that the hedging policy remains unchanged.

bull_case: Industry-leading, resilient operating margins (10.9% in H1 2026 despite a major fuel shock) demonstrate the structural benefit of IAG's diversified brand/market portfolio and transformation programmes
Scarce Heathrow and Madrid slots plus the transatlantic joint venture with American Airlines give British Airways and Iberia durable pricing power on the most profitable long-haul routes
IAG Loyalty (Avios) is a high-growth, high-margin, capital-light business on track toward ~€1bn operating profit, materially improving the Group's earnings mix and cash generation over time

Strong balance sheet (net leverage just 0.6x, ~€11.9bn liquidity) supports a large, ongoing shareholder return programme (€1.5bn excess-cash return, growing dividend) even through the current disruption

Current depressed share price (down after cautious FY2025 outlook commentary) may already discount much of the Middle East conflict and fuel-cost shock, offering upside if the conflict resolves or fuel prices normalize
bear_case: Middle East conflict has materially raised FY2026 fuel costs (guided up to €8.6bn from ~€7.0-7.4bn) and the Group recovers only ~60% of the increase, directly compressing margins and free cash flow versus original guidance

Aer Lingus requires a multi-year restructuring (job cuts, capacity reduction, base closures) to reach Group margin targets, and short-haul European markets face relentless low-cost-carrier capacity growth that limits pricing power across Vueling, Iberia and BA short-haul

Airlines remain fundamentally cyclical with high fixed costs and thin reported margins; any broader economic slowdown, further geopolitical shocks, or renewed fuel spike would disproportionately hit earnings

Heathrow expansion remains unresolved and contentious; IAG has said it will not support a third runway without charging-model reform, creating years of regulatory uncertainty around its most important hub

Management itself has flagged reduced visibility into near-term trading (Q2/Q3 2026), and guidance has already been cut multiple times in 2026 (capacity, fuel cost, capex, free cash flow), suggesting continued earnings volatility is likely
